seo_description: Khawar Shahzad and Arslan Khan on why marriage feels so difficult in Pakistan today: expectations, parents, social media and wedding costs.

guest.name: Arslan Khan
bio: Arslan Khan is a software engineer from Lahore with a computer science background and more than six years of experience. He was born and raised in Lahore, graduated in 2019, and has worked as a software engineer since then.
He is unmarried, and for him his passion is his profession.

summary: In Episode 15 of Muffled Minds, host Khawar Shahzad sits down with his friend Arslan Khan, a software engineer from Lahore, to talk about why marriage has become so difficult today: the expectations of boys and girls, the pressure from parents, and the cost of weddings in a Pakistan where social media sets the standard.

Arslan traces the problem from the start: parents begin the discussion, not the couple, and marriage is treated as a milestone to hit at 27 or 28 rather than a decision to be ready for, mentally as well as financially. He explains why clarity matters before the rishta — knowing what kind of partner you want, whether a housewife or an independent woman, and whether your families agree — and why compatibility, emotional and physical, matters more than the old checklist of salary, house and car. The conversation then turns to the competition between husband and wife: defined roles, appreciation, and why pointing fingers breaks a home that stands on two pillars.

The second half is about money and the screen: a wedding now costs 30 to 40 lakh, with seven or eight events copied from celebrities and TikTokers who got their decor free in collabs, and dowry forced on families in the name of izzat. Khawar and Arslan discuss separate living after marriage, the foreign trip before the wedding, and what social media does to the mind — the algorithm, the comparison, the unconscious copying of Western trends — and close with what a solution looks like: simple weddings, personal training in what you consume, and starting the change from yourself. It ends with the Fish Jar Q/A, where Arslan reveals his one ultimate wish.

takeaways: Check mental readiness, not just financial readiness: can you take responsibility, manage finances and give your partner space — before you decide to marry.
Be clear about what partner you want before the rishta: housewife or independent woman, and what your families expect — because the clash comes from unspoken expectations.
Compatibility matters more than the checklist: emotional and physical compatibility, and the honesty that nobody is perfect.
Marriage is not a competition: the home stands on two pillars, and if one is missing the system cannot work — appreciate what your partner does instead of counting what they did not.
A wedding costs 30 to 40 lakh today because we copy celebrities who got their decor free in collabs — and the bill lands on the husband and the father.
Dowry is forced in the name of izzat even when the boy says he does not want it — and fathers take loans for a daughter's wedding.
Separate living after marriage teaches responsibility: in your own house you see everything, and Islam itself divided the tent after marriage.
Social media trains you without you noticing: the algorithm shows you what you already believe, and the unconscious mind is more powerful than the conscious one.
Start the change from yourself: a simple wedding, training in what you consume, and the honesty that nobody will listen to a lecture — only an example.
